docs.title: django-spec-tasks
docs.text:
Run a django-service-specs spec as a background task: a durable run record, and a worker that re-checks through the kernel's dispatch.

from django_spec_tasks import enqueue

run_id = enqueue(orders, "refund_order", {"order": "7"}, actor=request.user)

enqueue runs the kernel's checks while the caller is on the stack, writes a SpecRun row, and asks a backend to run that id once the transaction commits. The worker claims the row, resolves the principal, calls dispatch and records the result on the row.

The queue decides where the code runs; the row decides whether it ran. A backend may lose a message or deliver it twice without consequence: a second copy finds the claim taken, and a sweep asks again for a run the queue lost. That is what lets one protocol hold Celery and Django Tasks.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install "django-spec-tasks[celery]"        # or
pip install "django-spec-tasks[django-tasks]"  # the backport, below Django 6.0

Add "django_spec_tasks" to INSTALLED_APPS and run migrate. Neither queue is a hard dependency, and Django 6.0 has django.tasks with no extra.

docs.title: A binding
docs.text:
A TaskBinding says which specs may run in the background, and how. Collaborators are objects passed here, never dotted paths in settings. Declare it in a spec_tasks module of an installed app, which the worker finds at startup:

# orders/spec_tasks.py
from django_spec_tasks import TaskBinding
from django_spec_tasks.backends.celery_backend import CeleryBackend

from orders.specs import order_specs

orders = TaskBinding(name="orders", registry=order_specs, backend=CeleryBackend())

Only name, registry and backend are required. The row records the binding's name, so do not rename one while it has runs pending.

docs.title: What a caller reads back
docs.text:
from django_spec_tasks import read_run

status = read_run(orders, run_id, request.user)
status.state  # RunState.SUCCEEDED
status.output  # what a JSON transport would have sent

read_run answers the run's owner, or whoever the binding's can_read allows, and refuses everyone else with one NotPermitted, whether or not the id exists. A run ends in one state, and a refusal is never a failure: the worker page has the table.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text: It is not a queue, a scheduler or a result store. The project owns its workers, its queues and the schedule that runs the sweep. There is no generic @task decorator, no retry policy, and no chaining or fan-out.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text:
• Backends: enqueueing, and choosing where a run executes.
  • Worker: the claim, the transaction, each ending, progress and the seams.
  • Operating: the sweep, reading a run, pruning, the admin.
  • With django-domain-events: composing with no import in either direction.
  • Reference: every public name.

docs.title: Enqueueing, and where a run executes
docs.text:
enqueue is the caller's half. A backend is the other: it asks a queue to call the worker with a run's id.

from django_spec_tasks import enqueue

run_id = enqueue(orders, "refund_order", {"order": "7"}, actor=request.user)

It returns the run's id as a string. actor is required: pass None for a system run, which the spec admits or refuses by its own permissions. Leaving the argument out is a TypeError, so an unauthenticated call cannot become a system run by omission.

docs.title: What enqueue refuses
docs.text:
Everything that can be refused while the caller is still on the stack is, and a refusal writes no row and sends nothing. A refusal spends no query: the kernel's prelude (check_call) reads the call and the principal and touches no table.

The call Raises a spec name the binding's registry does not hold LookupError, naming the binding and the name a spec with a file parameter, at any depth TypeError, naming the parameter an actor with no primary key, such as AnonymousUser TypeError, naming actor=None a deactivated actor PrincipalUnavailable an unknown, missing, mistyped or out-of-choices argument InvalidArguments a principal the spec's class-level permissions refuse NotPermitted a parameter named like one of the binding's pool seeds ImproperlyConfigured a parameter or carried value that JSON would change, or that a JSON column cannot hold (NaN, inf, a NUL character, half a surrogate pair) TypeError, naming the key

The check is the kernel's own, run with the binding's pool_seeds, so a seed collision is refused here exactly as the worker would refuse it. Nothing it grants crosses to the worker: the worker checks again.

The Validator does not run at enqueue. A stock one queries, needs the row it acts on, and its answer would not hold by the time a worker ran. The worker runs the whole of it.

docs.title: A file cannot cross
docs.text:
An upload is a live object, and a queue carries JSON. Save it to storage first and declare a parameter that holds its key:

key = default_storage.save(name, upload)
enqueue(imports, "import_orders", {"upload_key": key}, actor=request.user)

docs.title: What JSON would change
docs.text:
A queue stores JSON, and what it hands a worker is what survived. Django Tasks accepts some values that do not survive: a tuple comes back a list, bytes a string, a mapping with integer keys keeps them in one backend and loses them in the next. enqueue compares each parameter with its own round trip and refuses the difference, so the parameters a worker sees are the ones the caller wrote. Pass what a JSON body would carry.

binding.carry(actor), when set, is held to the same rule. Its result is recorded on the row and offered to the call context as carried, here and again in the worker, so a seed resolver reads the same value in both.

docs.title: When the message is sent
docs.text:
The row is written in the caller's transaction and the backend is asked on commit:

  • inside atomic, nothing is sent before the block commits;
  • if the block rolls back, nothing is sent and there is no row;
  • a backend that raises at commit (a broker that is down) does not cancel the callbacks the project registered after it, and leaves the row PENDING. The row is what makes the lost message recoverable, so the sweep asks again.

The callback is registered with robust=True on the alias the row was written to.

docs.title: Choosing a backend
docs.text: Name the backend on the binding. It is never chosen by what imports: django.tasks imports on any Django 6, and its default backend runs a task inline on the caller's thread, so a choice by availability would pick that in a project running Celery.

docs.title: Django Tasks
docs.text:
from django_spec_tasks.backends.django_tasks_backend import DjangoTasksBackend

orders = TaskBinding(name="orders", registry=registry, backend=DjangoTasksBackend())

DjangoTasksBackend(alias="default", queue=None) sends to the TASKS entry alias, and to queue on it when one is named. The framework is django.tasks from Django 6.0 and the django-tasks backport below it; install the backport with the django-tasks extra.

The module defines its task at the top level, as Django Tasks requires: a worker finds a task again by its dotted path, which must resolve to the task itself. The task is built against the default entry of TASKS, as any @task is, so TASKS needs one.

django.tasks on its own is not a deployment. Core ships ImmediateBackend, which runs the task on the caller's thread, and DummyBackend, which runs nothing; it has no worker and no durable backend. For production run django-tasks-db and its db_worker, or use Celery.

docs.title: Celery
docs.text:
from django_spec_tasks.backends.celery_backend import CeleryBackend

orders = TaskBinding(name="orders", registry=registry, backend=CeleryBackend())

CeleryBackend(queue=None) sends the run, with the run's id as Celery's task_id so a log line names the run. Install the celery extra.

The task is registered under the name django_spec_tasks.run_spec, spelled out and never derived from the module path, because messages already on a broker carry it. It is registered by importing the module, which the app does in ready() whenever celery is installed: a worker finds a message's task in its own registry, so a task built later, inside a call, would pass every test that sends and runs in one process and be missing from every real worker. Route it with task_routes, keyed by that name.

The package sets nothing else, each because the row already answers it:

Not set Why retries a re-run is the sweep's fresh enqueue of the same id, the same in either world acks_late your acknowledgement and visibility timeout apply; a second copy finds the claim taken result backend the result is on the row (ignore_result=True) beat the package schedules nothing routing no queue by default; task_routes decides

docs.title: What your project owns
docs.text:
The package asks a queue to call the worker; the deployment is yours.

Django Tasks Celery the worker process db_worker, or your backend's celery worker its queues TASKS entries and QUEUES task_routes, -Q the scheduler for the sweep a cron job or your scheduler Celery beat, or cron

docs.title: With django-domain-events
docs.text:
A project that records its events with django-domain-events can start a run from an event, fire an event from inside a run, and fire one when a run finishes. None of it needs an import in either package, and neither lists the other as a dependency or an extra.

They fit because both keep their record in a database row written inside whatever transaction the caller holds. An event and a run are each "intent, committed with the business change", so three seams on the binding and a few lines in the project are all the joining there is:

Seam What it is for here carry= records the caller's correlation id on the row at enqueue around_run= restores it, and the principal, in the worker around the service on_finish= fires an event inside the transaction of the run's terminal write

What was run. The recipe has been run against django-domain-events 0.14.1 by a throwaway probe on Django 6.1 and SQLite, not by a project: an event starting a run, a service and a finishing hook firing inside the worker's transaction, a lost claim, a killed worker, a replay, and attribution through attributed. The delayed run was read from the source and not run. The seams' own transaction behaviour is held by this package's tests, with a plain model standing in for the event log. Every domain-events name in the snippets is in django_domain_events.__all__ at 0.14.1.

docs.title: An event starts a run
docs.text:
A durable receiver calls enqueue from inside its delivery.

from django_domain_events import receiver
from django_spec_tasks import enqueue


@receiver(OrderPaid, key="orders.review_refund")
def review_refund(event: OrderPaid) -> None:
    enqueue(orders, "review_refund", {"order": event.order_id}, actor=None)

domain-events runs a durable receiver in the same transaction that records its acknowledgement, and enqueue writes the run row in the transaction it finds. So the row commits with the acknowledgement, and the backend is asked only after that commit.

  • A receiver that raises leaves no run and asks no backend: the row rolls back with the delivery, and the delivery is retried by domain-events as any failed one is.
  • A delivery whose acknowledgement is lost (the claim lapsed to another relay) leaves no run either.
  • A delivered event gives one run and one message. No dedup key is needed for that, on one condition.

The one-database condition. SpecRun and the event log must be on the same database. SpecRun is always on the default alias, and a system check refuses a router that sends it elsewhere. If the event log is written to another alias, the run row and the acknowledgement are two commits: a crash between them re-delivers the event and makes a second run. Give the receiver a dedup key of its own then, or move the log to the default alias.

A replay is a new run. replay_events reopens a finished delivery, the receiver runs again, and enqueue writes another row. That is what a replay asks for: the event is owed again, and what an event is owed is a run. It is a statement here and not a guard. idempotent does not change it, since that only decides whether the sweep may requeue a run whose worker was lost; if the second call should change nothing, that comes from the service's own logic.

An event's actor is attribution, not authorization. The receiver chooses the principal itself, or passes actor=None and lets the spec answer for a system run. The event is never handed to the permission check as a grant. None is admitted only by a spec whose permissions admit it, and a gated spec refuses it at enqueue with NotPermitted. Whoever fired the event may have acted with a role the worker will not find, and the worker re-checks everything enqueue did, so a run is authorized now or it is AUTHORIZATION_LAPSED.

Inside a receiver current_scope() holds only what an enclosing attributed block set, so a run started from a receiver carries a correlation id only if the receiver opened such a block.

docs.title: A service fires inside a run
docs.text:
fire() writes into the transaction it finds. Under the worker's outer transaction, which a spec with atomic=True gets, the event commits with the run's terminal state, and a worker killed before the commit leaves neither the event nor the service's work, only a RUNNING row for the sweep.

from dataclasses import dataclass

from django_domain_events import event, fire
from django_service_specs import Parameter, Parameters, ServiceSpec, Unrestricted


@event
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class OrderRefunded:
    order_id: str


def refund_order(*, order: str) -> None:
    ...  # the work
    fire(OrderRefunded(order_id=order))


refund = ServiceSpec(
    service=refund_order,
    atomic=True,
    permissions=[Unrestricted()],
    reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("order", "string", required=True)),
)

Under atomic=False, fire() warns that it ran outside a transaction, as it would anywhere: the event commits when it is written, and the terminal state is a second fact. A spec that wants its events tied to its work declares atomic=True or opens its own transaction.

A worker has no request, so an event fired there carries no actor and no correlation id. Filling the two seams is enough:

from uuid import UUID, uuid4

from django_domain_events import attributed, current_scope
from django_spec_tasks import TaskBinding


def carry_correlation(actor):
    return {"correlation_id": str(current_scope().correlation_id or uuid4())}


def attribute(run, principal):
    correlation = run.carried.get("correlation_id")
    return attributed(
        actor=principal,
        correlation_id=UUID(correlation) if correlation else None,
    )


orders = TaskBinding(
    name="orders",
    registry=registry,
    backend=backend,
    carry=carry_correlation,
    around_run=attribute,
)

carry is called by enqueue, in the caller's scope, and the mapping is stored on the row, so it must survive JSON: a value JSON would change is refused there. around_run is called in the worker with the row and the resolved principal, and is entered before dispatch and left after present. Anything the service fires between them has the actor and the correlation id. This is the same shape as domain-events' own AROUND_DELIVERY hook for receivers.

carry_correlation mints an id when the caller has none, so a run enqueued with no ambient correlation still fires every event of the run under one id of its own, the finish event below included. Left to attributed, which also mints one when it is given none, each seam would get a different id.

docs.title: A run finishing fires an event
docs.text:
on_finish(run) runs inside the transaction of the run's terminal write, after around_run has left. An event fired there exists if and only if the state committed.

@event
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RunFinished:
    run_id: str
    spec: str
    state: str


def announce(run):
    correlation = run.carried.get("correlation_id")
    with attributed(correlation_id=UUID(correlation) if correlation else None):
        fire(RunFinished(run_id=str(run.pk), spec=run.spec_name, state=str(run.state)))


orders = TaskBinding(..., carry=carry_correlation, around_run=attribute, on_finish=announce)

What that guarantees:

  • A refusal fires it too. Under atomic=True the service's work rolls back first, then the refused state and the event commit together in a transaction of their own.
  • A lost claim fires nothing. A worker whose lease lapsed finds the terminal write matching no row, so the write does not happen, on_finish is not called, and under atomic=True what the service fired rolls back as well. Under atomic=False what the service fired stands, and no finish event exists.
  • The sweep fires it for its endings. A run the sweep ends ABANDONED, or SPEC_UNAVAILABLE while its binding is still registered, calls the same hook, in the transaction of its write, on a row of the same shape as the worker's.
  • A hook that raises takes the write with it. The event it fired before raising is gone and the run stays RUNNING. The sweep's ending calls the same hook, so the run stays there, counted in the sweep's errors, until the hook stops raising.

An event fired from on_finish is outside around_run, so it has no actor from that seam. announce above takes its correlation from the row.

docs.title: A delayed run
docs.text:
domain-events lets a receiver declare when its delivery runs: due= takes a timedelta, counted from the event, or a callable returning an aware datetime. A receiver declared with due= that calls enqueue is a delayed spec run, and nothing in either package is a scheduler.

from datetime import timedelta


@receiver(OfferSent, key="offers.expire", due=timedelta(hours=48))
def expire_offer(event: OfferSent) -> None:
    enqueue(offers, "expire_offer", {"offer": event.offer_id}, actor=None)

Periodic work stays with the project's own scheduler, which calls enqueue or sweep_runs.

docs.title: Why a run is not a delivery
docs.text:
A design that runs each spec as a delivery, with the worker a receiver and no SpecRun, looks smaller. It is not the same thing:

  • A lapsed lease re-runs without asking. domain-events owes any claimed delivery whose lease has lapsed, and nothing in that path reads whether repeating the receiver is safe. A receiver killed mid-call is called again. This package has a state table so that a lost worker is read against idempotent: an idempotent run goes back to PENDING, any other is ABANDONED.
  • It needs a relay process. A deployment whose only queue is Celery or Django Tasks owns none.
  • It still needs a row. A delivery has no place for the presented result or the refusal, which are what a caller reads back.
  • It couples the packages. Neither lists the other, and the recipe keeps it so; a run that was a delivery would need one to import the other's worker.

So the packages meet at a row each: an event can start a run, and a run can fire an event, and neither owns the other's record.

docs.title: Operating
docs.text: Four things keep a deployment honest: a sweep that answers runs the queue lost, a read side that says who may see a run, pruning that deletes old rows, and an admin that shows them. None of them is scheduled by this package. A project runs the sweep and the prune the way it runs anything periodic: a Celery beat entry, cron, or its platform's scheduler.

docs.title: The sweep
docs.text:
from django_spec_tasks import sweep_runs

report = sweep_runs()  # SweepReport(reasked=0, requeued=1, abandoned=0, unavailable=0, errors=0)

or, from a scheduler that runs commands:

python manage.py sweep_spec_runs
python manage.py sweep_spec_runs --limit 200

The command prints how many rows moved where: Swept spec runs: 1 requeued, 0 abandoned, 0 spec unavailable, 3 asked again, 0 errors.

A queue may lose a message, so the row is the record and the sweep is how a lost run is found.

Row Outcome PENDING, its binding's grace past the last ask the backend is asked again; the claim stops a second run RUNNING past lease_expires_at, the spec declares idempotent=True, attempts < max_attempts back to PENDING, and the backend is asked the same, attempts >= max_attempts ABANDONED: a run that keeps killing its worker must not loop the same, idempotent is False or undeclared ABANDONED any of the above, the binding or the spec is gone SPEC_UNAVAILABLE

idempotent is read from the registered spec when the sweep runs, never from the row, so a spec whose declaration changed answers with what it declares now. Undeclared is not True: a spec that says nothing is abandoned, not retried.

grace is measured from asked_at, the last time a backend was asked for the row: when it was created, requeued or re-asked. So a queue that is backed up, or down, gets one more message per grace, not one per sweep. Size it to how long the queue may fall behind.

A row whose binding this process does not know has no grace of its own, so a pending one waits out the default (TaskBinding.grace's default of ten minutes) before it is ended. A sweep running on code from before a binding was added would otherwise end every run of it the moment it was written. Keep the process that sweeps on the same code as the one that enqueues.

docs.title: What a lapse leaves behind
docs.text:
It depends on the spec:

  • Under atomic=True the database effects rolled back with the worker, so idempotent decides only whether external effects (an email, a call to a payment provider) may happen twice.
  • Under atomic=False the work may have happened. ABANDONED there means unknown: the sweep cannot tell whether the run finished its work and died before it wrote the state.

A worker that is slow rather than dead is refused at its own terminal write once the sweep has moved the row. Under atomic=True its effects roll back; under atomic=False they stand. So size a binding's lease to its longest run.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
• Every move is a compare-and-swap on (state, attempts). Two sweeps agree on one transition, and a worker that claimed the row after the sweep read it is not overwritten. An ask is conditioned on asked_at as well, so two sweeps send one message.
  • on_finish runs for ABANDONED and SPEC_UNAVAILABLE, in the transaction with the state write, so every terminal state fires it. If it raises, that row's write rolls back, the error is logged and counted in errors, and the sweep carries on. The row stays as it was, on every sweep, until the hook stops raising: fix the hook, and the next sweep ends it.
  • A backend that raises is counted in errors. Its row stays PENDING (a requeued one too), and the ask is already stamped, so the sweep asks again once grace has passed.
  • A sweep is bounded, and one binding cannot starve another. Each binding is walked apart, its lapsed rows before its pending ones, longest waiting first, batch_size at a time. limit caps how many rows one sweep looks at for one binding, so a dead queue or a broken hook holds back only its own binding.

docs.title: Reading a run
docs.text:
from django_spec_tasks import read_run

status = read_run(orders, run_id, request.user)

read_run returns a frozen RunStatus: id, state, kind, output, progress, progress_message, refusal_code, refusal_detail, created_at, finished_at. It never carries params, carried, traceback, actor_pk or refusal_class. The call's arguments and its presented output are as sensitive as the call, so:

  1. the run's owner reads it, when the principal is not deactivated; or
  2. the binding's can_read(principal, run) says yes.

Anything else raises NotPermitted. So do an unknown id, a malformed one, and a run of another binding, with the same message, so an id cannot be probed for whether it exists. A deactivated principal is refused on both paths. A system run has no owner, so only can_read reads it.

state_of(binding, run_id) is for trusted callers: the state alone, with no principal, or None for an id that is not that binding's.

docs.title: Pruning
docs.text:
python manage.py prune_spec_runs --older-than 30

Deletes runs in a terminal state that finished more than the given number of days ago, in batches. It never deletes a PENDING or RUNNING row, however old. There is no default age, so the argument is required: how long to keep a run is the project's decision.

docs.title: Admin
docs.text:
SpecRun is registered read-only. Nobody adds, changes or deletes a run, and there are no actions (an admin action skips the change permission). The list shows state, spec, binding, actor, attempts and times, and filters by state and binding. params, carried and output are hidden because they hold what the call was given and returned; the traceback shows, for triage.

To show the payloads, subclass the admin and set the flag:

from django.contrib import admin

from django_spec_tasks.admin import SpecRunAdmin
from django_spec_tasks.models.spec_run import SpecRun


class PayloadSpecRunAdmin(SpecRunAdmin):
    show_payloads = True


admin.site.unregister(SpecRun)
admin.site.register(SpecRun, PayloadSpecRunAdmin)

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Every name on this page is in the API reference.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text: Everything below is exported from django_spec_tasks directly, except the two backends, which stay on their own paths because each imports an optional queue. Kernel names a binding reads, such as SpecRegistry and resolve_principal, are documented on the kernel's site.

docs.title: System checks
docs.text:
Registered by the app's config, so a project gets them by listing "django_spec_tasks" in INSTALLED_APPS.

  • django_spec_tasks.E001: a database router sends SpecRun away from the default alias. The kernel's transaction opens on the default alias, and the worker needs the row inside it.

docs.title: Management commands
docs.text:
• sweep_spec_runs: see sweep_runs.
  • prune_spec_runs --older-than DAYS: see prune_runs.

docs.title: enqueue
docs.text:
enqueue(
    binding: TaskBinding, spec_name: str, params: Mapping[str, Any], *, actor: Any
) -> str

Record a run of spec_name and ask the binding's backend to execute it on commit.

Everything that can be refused while the caller is still on the stack is refused here, and a refusal writes no row and sends nothing. What is left is decided by the worker, which checks again through the kernel's dispatch: a grant cannot cross a process, so none is carried.

actor is required. None is the declared system run, which a spec admits or refuses by its own permissions; leaving it out is a TypeError, so an unauthenticated call cannot become a system run by omission.

The Validator does not run here. A stock one queries, needs the row it acts on, and its answer would not hold by the time a worker ran.

Returns:

Type Description str

The run's id, as a string. A backend that carries a task id is given this one.

Raises:

Type Description LookupError

The binding's registry holds no spec of that name.

TypeError

The spec takes a file parameter; actor is a principal with no primary key (an anonymous user); or params or the carried values would change on their way through JSON.

PrincipalUnavailable

actor is deactivated.

InvalidArguments

params do not fit the spec.

NotPermitted

actor fails the spec's class-level permissions.

ImproperlyConfigured

A parameter collides with one of the binding's pool seeds.

docs.title: read_run
docs.text:
read_run(binding: TaskBinding, run_id: str, principal: Any) -> RunStatus

What principal may see of a run: its status, never what it was asked.

The call's params and its presented output are as sensitive as the call itself, so the default reader is the run's owner. binding.can_read(principal, run) widens that. A principal that is deactivated is refused either way: it never acts.

A run that is not this principal's, an id nobody wrote, a malformed id and another binding's run all raise the same NotPermitted with the same message, so an id cannot be probed for whether it exists. A system run has no owner, so only can_read reads it.

Raises:

Type Description NotPermitted

For every refusal above.

docs.title: state_of
docs.text:
state_of(binding: TaskBinding, run_id: str) -> RunState | None

The state of one of binding's runs, with no principal asked.

For a caller that is trusted, such as a queue reporting on a run it enqueued. It answers None for an id that is not this binding's, or not an id at all. Anything a person may reach goes through read_run.

docs.title: TaskBinding dataclass
docs.text:
A registry served as background tasks, with everything a queue needs beside it.

Collaborators are objects passed here, never dotted paths in settings. A seam that takes a run is handed the SpecRun row, typed Any because nothing here imports a model: that is what keeps this class importable before the app registry is ready.

Constructing one registers it under its name, since a worker has only the name a row recorded. Autodiscovery of each installed app's spec_tasks module is what makes every binding known in a worker that imported Django.

Attributes:

Name Type Description name str

Recorded on every row, so it must not change while runs are pending.

registry SpecRegistry

Where enqueue and the worker find a spec by name.

backend TaskBackend

Where a run's code executes.

resolve_actor Callable[[str], Any]

Turns a row's actor_pk into the principal. Raises PrincipalUnavailable for anyone who may no longer act.

pool_seeds PoolSeeds

The same set at enqueue and in the worker, so the prelude's seed check agrees between them.

lease timedelta

How long a claimed run may take. Sized to the binding's longest run: a worker past it is refused at its terminal write.

grace timedelta

How long a PENDING row waits, from the last time a backend was asked for it, before the sweep asks again. Sized to how long the queue may back up: each ask past it is one more message.

max_attempts int

How many claims an idempotent run gets before it is abandoned.

max_output_bytes int

Past this, a run ends OUTPUT_TOO_LARGE. Output is never truncated.

can_read Callable[[Any, Any], bool] | None

(principal, run) -> bool, consulted beside the run's owner.

progress_using str | None

A database alias progress is written through, which is what makes it visible during an atomic=True run. A second connection to the same database: on any other it finds no row, and writes nothing.

carry Callable[[Any], Mapping[str, Any]] | None

(actor) -> JSON mapping, recorded on the row at enqueue and handed to the call context in both processes.

around_run Callable[[Any, Any], AbstractContextManager[Any]] | None

(run, principal) -> context manager around dispatch and present.

on_finish Callable[[Any], None] | None

(run) -> None, inside the transaction of the terminal write.

docs.title: named classmethod
docs.text:
named(name: str) -> TaskBinding | None

The binding registered under name, or None.

A row naming no binding is a rolling deploy rather than a bug, so an unknown name is an answer here and not an exception.

docs.title: clear_registry classmethod
docs.text:

docs.title: TaskBackend
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Where a run's code executes.

The row is the record, so a backend may lose a message without consequence: the sweep asks again. It may also deliver one twice or late, and the claim stops the second copy. That is what keeps this a single method, and what lets one protocol hold Django Tasks and Celery.

docs.title: enqueue
docs.text:
enqueue(run_id: str) -> None

Arrange for run_spec(run_id) to be called somewhere.

docs.title: CeleryBackend
docs.text:
Hands a run to a Celery worker.

queue names the queue to send to; None leaves routing to the project's task_routes, keyed by the stable task name. The package sets no retry, no late acknowledgement, no result backend and no schedule, each because the row already answers it: a second copy of a message finds the claim taken, a lost one is asked for again by the sweep, and the result is on the row.

Send the run, with its id as Celery's task_id so a log line names the run.

docs.title: DjangoTasksBackend
docs.text:
Hands a run to Django's Tasks framework.

Name the backend in the binding; it is never chosen by what imports. django.tasks imports on any Django 6, and its default backend runs a task inline on the caller's thread, so choosing by availability would pick that in a project running Celery.

alias is the TASKS entry to send to, queue the queue on it; None leaves the framework's default. The module's task is built against the default entry, as any @task is, so TASKS needs one.

docs.title: run_spec
docs.text:
run_spec(run_id: str) -> None

Run the row run_id names, once, whatever number of messages name it.

Both backends call this. It returns nothing, and no retry policy of a queue's applies: whether a run may run again is read from the row, by the sweep.

A message for a row that is not PENDING costs one query and runs nothing. Otherwise the row is claimed, the principal resolved, and the spec called through the kernel's dispatch and present, so the worker re-checks everything enqueue checked and the Validator runs for the first time. The row ends in the state run_state_for gives what was raised, or in SUCCEEDED with what was presented, or in OUTPUT_TOO_LARGE. A service whose target is gone never ran, and ends REFUSED; a selector finding nothing has answered, and ends SUCCEEDED, each with kind="not_found".

Under atomic=True one transaction holds around_run, dispatch, present, the terminal write and on_finish, so the service's work and the row's state commit as one fact, and a worker that dies before the commit has left nothing but a RUNNING row. A refusal rolls that transaction back first, then writes its state and runs on_finish in a transaction of its own. Under atomic=False, and for a selector, no transaction surrounds the call, and only the write and on_finish share one.

A write finding the row is no longer this attempt's writes nothing and rolls its own transaction back: a worker that lost its claim cannot commit.

Only an Exception is an ending. A BaseException is the worker dying, and passes through untouched, as does anything on_finish raises: both leave the row RUNNING. The sweep answers a dead worker's. It calls the same hook, so a hook that always raises keeps its row RUNNING until it stops raising.

docs.title: run_state_for
docs.text:
run_state_for(error: BaseException) -> RunState

The RunState error ends a run in.

Every refusal has one, a subclass a later release adds included: it takes its nearest listed base's, so a new refusal of the call is INVALID and a new refusal by the operation REFUSED. Anything else is FAILED: an exception nobody declared is a bug, and FAILED is never the answer to a refusal.

docs.title: sweep_runs
docs.text:
sweep_runs(*, limit: int = 1000, batch_size: int = 100) -> SweepReport

Answer the runs the queue lost and end the ones whose worker did not come back.

Run it on a schedule the project owns: a beat entry, cron, the platform's scheduler. This package ships none, because whether a queue is one's own is not for a library to assume.

Row Outcome PENDING, grace past its last ask the backend is asked again; the claim stops a second run RUNNING past its lease, spec declares idempotent=True, attempts to spare back to PENDING and the backend is asked the same, attempts >= max_attempts ABANDONED: a poison run must not loop the same, idempotent False or undeclared ABANDONED either, binding or spec gone SPEC_UNAVAILABLE

idempotent is read off the registered spec now, never off the row, so a spec whose declaration changed answers with what it declares today. None is undeclared and does not read as True.

Every transition is a compare-and-swap on (state, attempts), so two sweeps agree and a worker that claimed the row meanwhile is not overwritten. An ask is stamped on asked_at before the backend hears it, conditioned on the value read as well, so two sweeps send one message, and a row waits out its grace again whether or not the backend took it. A backend that raises is counted in errors, and the sweep carries on.

on_finish runs for ABANDONED and SPEC_UNAVAILABLE in the transaction with the write. One that raises takes the write back: it is counted in errors, and the row stays as it was, on every sweep, until the hook stops raising.

Each binding is walked apart, its lapsed rows first and then its pending ones, longest waiting first, batch_size at a time, and limit is its own, so a binding whose queue is dead or whose hook is broken holds back nothing but itself.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default limit int

The most rows one sweep looks at for one binding.

1000 batch_size int

How many rows are read from the database at once.

100

Returns:

Type Description SweepReport

What was done, counted by outcome.

docs.title: prune_runs
docs.text:
prune_runs(*, older_than: timedelta, batch_size: int = 1000) -> int

Delete runs that finished more than older_than ago, and no others.

A run that is still PENDING or RUNNING is never deleted, however old: it is the sweep's to answer, and deleting it would lose work. A finished run without a finished_at is left too, since there is no age to measure. Retention is the project's call, so there is no default age.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default older_than timedelta

How long ago a run must have finished.

required batch_size int

How many rows one delete takes, so no statement is unbounded.

1000

Returns:

Type Description int

How many rows were deleted.

docs.title: SpecRunAdmin
docs.text:
Bases: ModelAdmin

Runs, to look at and never to change.

Nothing here adds, changes or deletes a row, and there are no actions: an admin action skips the change permission, so an action that deleted would delete for a user who could not. params, carried and output hold what the call was given and what it returned, so they are hidden, and refused as URL lookups, since a count of results would answer a guess; a project that wants them in its admin sets show_payloads on a subclass. The traceback shows, because triage needs it.

docs.title: SpecRun
docs.text:
Bases: Model

One call of a spec: what was asked, whose claim it is under, and how it ended.

Every column is the call or the queue's bookkeeping about it, and none copies a declaration: idempotent and atomic are read from the registered spec. All of them land in the first migration, since a column added later is empty for every earlier run.

output and refusal_detail hold what a presenter and a refusal produced, so they encode through DjangoJSONEncoder: a refusal's messages may be lazy strings, and a spec with no presenter hands back its value as it is. params and carried keep the default encoder, because enqueue asserts that they survive a JSON round trip.

state is indexed by the three composite indexes, each leading on it.

docs.title: RunState
docs.text:
Bases: TextChoices

Where a run is. PENDING and RUNNING are live; the rest are terminal.

A state stays coarse: the row's refusal_class and refusal_code say which refusal ended a run. The whole table lands in the first release, because a state added later is missing from every run before it.

Each value spells its name, so a value read back off a row as a plain string compares equal and hashes equal, and run.state in TERMINAL_STATES holds.

docs.title: TERMINAL_STATES module-attribute
docs.text:
TERMINAL_STATES: frozenset[RunState] = frozenset(RunState) - {
    RunState.PENDING,
    RunState.RUNNING,
}

Every state a run does not leave. A run in one is what pruning may delete.

docs.title: RunStatus dataclass
docs.text:
What a reader of a run is shown: how it went, and none of what it was asked.

params, carried, traceback, actor_pk and refusal_class are left out on purpose. The call's arguments are as sensitive as the call, a traceback names code, and the owner is who is asking.

docs.title: SweepReport dataclass
docs.text:
What one sweep did, counted by outcome.

reasked is a backend call and not a transition: a PENDING row the queue seems to have lost stays PENDING. requeued, abandoned and unavailable are transitions. errors counts rows left as they were because a backend or an on_finish raised.

docs.title: The worker
docs.text:
run_spec(run_id) runs one row: it claims it, calls the spec through the kernel's dispatch, and records how the call ended, in one transaction when the spec says atomic=True. Progress under atomic=True is invisible until that transaction commits, unless the binding names a progress_using alias: a report written on the connection holding the transaction cannot be read from any other, which is the point of the transaction and the cost of writing to the row.

Both backends call this function with one string and read nothing back. It takes no retries and returns no result: whether a run may run again is read from the row.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1. Read. A row that is not PENDING ends the call here. A redelivered message costs one query and no run, whatever the spec declares.
  2. Find. The binding by name and the spec in its registry. Either missing ends the row SPEC_UNAVAILABLE, from PENDING, with attempts unchanged, and {"message": ...} in refusal_detail naming what is missing.
  3. Claim. One conditional UPDATE to RUNNING, committed alone before anything runs. Losing it ends the call. Two copies of a message cannot both win, and a copy cannot run a row another attempt finished.
  4. Resolve. actor_pk null means the principal is None, never AnonymousUser, and a spec gated on a principal refuses it. Otherwise binding.resolve_actor(actor_pk).
  5. Run. dispatch, then present, inside around_run. Everything enqueue checked is checked again, and the Validator runs for the first time.
  6. Record. A write conditioned on (pk, state, attempts), then on_finish, in one transaction.

The call is a task call: call_transport(call_context) reads "task", and whatever carry recorded at enqueue is at call_context["carried"], where a PoolSeeds resolver can read it.

docs.title: The transaction
docs.text:
Spec What wraps what ServiceSpec with atomic=True one transaction around around_run, dispatch, present, the terminal write and on_finish ServiceSpec with atomic=False no outer transaction; the terminal write and on_finish take their own SelectorSpec nothing to roll back, so as atomic=False

So under atomic=True the service's work and the run's state are one fact. A worker dying before the commit leaves no row of the service's, and a RUNNING run the sweep answers.

A refusal or an exception rolls that transaction back first, then writes its state and runs on_finish in a transaction of its own, so the state and what it fires still commit together.

The window that remains. An atomic=False spec's committed work and its terminal write are two facts. A worker dying between them leaves a RUNNING row the sweep ends ABANDONED, with the work done. That is what atomic=False means, and it is the right choice for a call one transaction should not span, such as an agent run.

A lost claim commits nothing. Past its lease a run may be handed to another worker or ended by the sweep. The terminal write then matches no row: it logs a warning and writes nothing, nothing fires, and under atomic=True the service's work rolls back with it. Under atomic=False the work stands. So a binding's lease is sized to its longest run.

docs.title: How a run ends
docs.text:
Raised State Why NotPermitted, PermissionCheckDenied AUTHORIZATION_LAPSED authorized at enqueue, refused now: access changed, the code did not break PrincipalUnavailable AUTHORIZATION_LAPSED deleted, malformed or deactivated in the window InvalidArguments INVALID the Validator runs only here DispatchError, and any later subclass INVALID a refusal of the call ServiceValidationError INVALID the service's word for bad input ServiceNotFound REFUSED the target vanished ActionUnavailable, ServiceConflict CONFLICT terminal; ActionUnavailable leaves its code AdditionalInputRequired INPUT_REQUIRED nobody to ask; the remedy is a new enqueue carrying the answer ServiceError, and any later subclass REFUSED the operation refused on its own terms

run_state_for(error) is this table. Anything else is FAILED, and FAILED is never the answer to a refusal.

Every row of the table records:

Column Holds refusal_class the class's name, a project's own subclass included refusal_code its code, where it has one refusal_detail {"message": ..., "errors": ..., "schema": ...}

errors is the field errors of an InvalidArguments or a ServiceValidationError, and schema is what an AdditionalInputRequired asks for; each is null otherwise. A refusal carrying a detail no JSON column could store keeps its state and its message, with both null.

A FAILED run has traceback and leaves the refusal columns null: a reader is shown refusal_detail and never traceback, so a fault's words stay where only an operator looks.

docs.title: The result
docs.text:
SUCCEEDED records kind, and output, which is present(spec, result): what a JSON transport would have sent, stamped with package_version since it is a contract. instance_pk keeps the target's identity. kind is "instance", "list" or "not_found". A selector that finds nothing has answered, so it ends SUCCEEDED with kind="not_found" and no output. A service whose target is gone never ran, so it ends REFUSED, with kind="not_found" and refusal_class="ServiceNotFound", as a ServiceNotFound the service raises itself does: a refund of a deleted order must not read as a refund that happened.

The bound. Past max_output_bytes, measured as the column writes it, the run ends OUTPUT_TOO_LARGE with {"size": ..., "limit": ...} in refusal_detail, and output stays null. Under atomic=True the work rolls back with it, so the caller reads a clean refusal. Under atomic=False the work stands, and the state says the result was not stored. Output is never truncated.

Output a JSON column cannot hold, which is a presenter's bug, ends FAILED, as any exception nobody declared does. That counts NaN, inf, a NUL character and half a surrogate pair, which Postgres refuses and SQLite mostly stores. A refusal keeps its state however it reads: a message and a traceback lose what no text column holds, a code is clipped to its column, and a detail no column could hold is left out.

docs.title: Progress
docs.text:
A service declaring progress gets a reporter that writes to the row, for as long as this attempt holds it. With a total, the progress column holds the fraction done; without one, the service's own unit. message lands in progress_message, and meta is dropped.

Spec progress_using Read from another connection atomic=False, or a selector unset at once atomic=True unset only after the run commits, and never if it rolls back atomic=True an alias at once, on a database that lets a second connection write

A report that cannot be written is logged and dropped: progress never ends a run. SQLite has one writer, so under atomic=True an alias's write waits for the service's and fails once the service has written anything.

Progress increases within one dispatch. A claim clears both columns, so an idempotent spec run again starts from nothing rather than from what the attempt before it reported.

docs.title: The seams
docs.text:
around_run(run, principal) is entered before dispatch and left after present, and is handed what the call raises. It may not swallow it: with no result to record, a run whose seam swallowed its exception ends FAILED rather than SUCCEEDED with nothing to show.

on_finish(run) runs inside the terminal transaction and reads the row as a reader would. Raising from it is a bug in the project: the terminal write rolls back with it, and the exception reaches the worker. The row stays RUNNING, and the sweep's own ending calls the same hook, so a hook that always raises keeps the row RUNNING and counted in the sweep's errors until it stops raising.

docs.title: Exceptions the worker does not catch
docs.text: A BaseException is the worker dying: it passes through untouched, rolling back whatever transaction is open, and leaves the row RUNNING. So does anything raised while recording the ending, since nothing could record that either.
